Maya Lopez: Schedule 2-hour runtime deep dive and private deploy checklist by 2027-03-12
Tom Patel: Provide sample anonymized prompt set and SLO targets by 2027-03-08
action_items: Alex Chen - Send pricing for hosted vs dedicated with example TCO for 1M tokens/month (due 2027-03-09)
Maya Lopez - Prepare short runbook for VPC deployment and KMS integration (due 2027-03-12)

summary: Introductory demo and scoping session for a Stratus pilot to evaluate open models from Redwood's catalog. Covered selection heuristics, benchmark plan, compatibility matrix mapping to their on-prem requirements, and security controls (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Agreed next steps around bench artifacts and a follow-up deep dive for private deployment.
topics: Model catalog filtering and selection heuristics
Hosting options: hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC)
Security: KMS, audit logs, SOC2 and data residency
Runtime optimizations: batching, caching, quantization suggestions
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-03-05 16:00 PT | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Lopez (Redwood SE), Tom Patel (CTO - Stratus), Priya Nair (ML Engineer), Sara Gomez (Head of Security), Liam O'Rourke (Product)

00:00 Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex Chen from Redwood inference, i'm the AE on the account. We'll kick off with a quick agenda: catalog walkthrough, bench scope, security checklist, and next steps. Maya will demo the console and bench planner.
00:22 Tom (CTO): Thanks, Alex. We're excited—short context: Stratus is trying to replace a black-box vendor for clinical summarization, we want more control on latency and residency. Primary concerns are throughput and PHI handling.
00:37 Priya (ML): Hey, i run the model experiments. For the pilot we need to evaluate a handful of open LLMs for summarization quality, latency at 512 tokens, and cost projections. Also need guidance on quantization tradeoffs because we might run GPUs in-house.
00:55 Maya (SE): Great, that's exactly what the catalog + bench flow is for. I'll show how to pick candidate models using inputs like max context, tokenization, and supported kernels. Also how Redwood's compatibility matrix flags runtime kernels and quant profiles.
01:12 Sara (Security): Quick callout from security: we need to understand KMS options (customer-managed keys), audit log retention, and SOC2 scope for the private control plane. Also data egress and on-prem isolation concerns.
01:28 Alex (AE): Noted. We'll surface the SOC2 docs and the KMS integration guide. Ok Maya over to you for demo.

03:05 Maya (SE): Opening the console - this is the model catalog view. You can filter by task type (summarization), latency tier, and hardware compatibility. We're going to pick three candidate families: a mid-sized 13B, a 6B tuned-for-safety, and a 2.7B low-latency baseline for smoke tests.
03:34 Priya (ML): Are those quant-friendly? We currently prefer int8-ish profiles but might go to 4-bit for cost.
03:44 Maya (SE): Yes, the catalog shows compatibility badges: native float kernels, int8 quant profiles available, and a 'quant-validated' flag for models we bench on Ampere and on-prem RTX class. Note: sometimes the badge says 'quant experimental'—that means we've seen functional regressions on some datasets, you'll want to include your clinical prompts in the bench.
04:12 Tom (CTO): One of our constraints is a 95th percentile latency < 400ms at 512 tokens for synchronous summarization. Is that realistic with open models?
04:26 Maya (SE): For hosted inference on high tier GPUs we can often hit that for the smaller families. For larger models, you'll need to tradeoff with batching and cold-starts. On dedicated pools we can tune sequence packing and kernel selection to push down tail latency. We'll include a latency-vs-cost curve in the bench.

06:00 Maya (SE): Switching to the bench planner—here we map prompts to evaluation slices and specify SLOs. You can input your sample prompt set or we can generate synthetic clinical snippets. For acceptance we'll measure ROUGE/QA metrics and also latency, p95, and cost per 1k tokens.
06:25 Priya (ML): We'll upload an anonymized prompt set. Any constraints on size? We have about 2k prompts but can start with 500 representative ones.
06:33 Maya (SE): 500 is perfect for the first pass. Also upload a small adversarial set for safety checks.

08:10 Alex (AE): On cost modeling—I'll be conservative. For hosted we'll show token-based pricing projections, for dedicated we'll give reserved GPU TCO with throughput curves. We'll include a chart showing when dedicated becomes cheaper based on tokens/month.
08:30 Tom (CTO): And for private on-prem deployment, do you support our KMS / HSM? We have an AWS KMS account and an internal HSM for keys.
08:40 Maya (SE): We support KMS integrations for private control plane and can integrate customer-managed keys via our connector. HSM for on-prem is more of a custom engagement, but we've done it with customers—will require a security design review and a small deployment ops project.

10:02 Sara (Security): On audit logs, we need immutable logs for model invocations and admin actions for at least 1 year. Also SSO with SAML and fine-grained RBAC.
10:16 Alex (AE): We have SOC2 and SAML SSO; retention for logs is configurable in the private offering. I'll attach the SOC2 certificate and an audit log sample.

11:05 Maya (SE): Back to the compatibility matrix: each model row lists supported kernels, max_context, KV cache behavior, and whether we've validated prefix caching. Important: prefix/KV caching gives huge cost reductions for chat-style workloads, less so for standalone summarization but still beneficial for templates. Our bench will toggle KV caching on/off to measure delta.
11:40 Priya (ML): Could you clarify what you mean by KV cache behaviour? Sometimes the transcripts call it a 'K-V cash' in docs and we've seen confusion.
11:52 Maya (SE): Yeah that's a transcription artifact—it's KV cache. It's about how the runtime stores key/value pairs for attention so repeated prefixes don't recompute. For your workload we expect some gains if you have repeated clinical headers.

13:30 Tom (CTO): For the bench, we need to include private data constraints. We'll provide anonymized prompts but we also want to run a small in-house bench on our hardware. Can Redwood provide the bench harness to run locally?
13:47 Maya (SE): Absolutely. We can provide a bench harness (it's a lightweight runner + model variants) and guidance on kernel builds. For private runs we'll share an evaluation runner and a small docker image. We'll also include config for our quant profiles.

15:20 Priya (ML): About model rollouts—if we pin a model version in production, is there an automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if capacity spikes?
15:31 Alex (AE): Yes, smart routing policies allow you to define fallbacks by policy: latency-first, cost-first, or mixed. You can set canary percentages and automatic fallback to compatible variants if the preferred model is unavailable. We'll demo that in the follow-up.

17:00 Maya (SE): Showing the compatibility map now—notice how a model can be 'runtime compatible' on Ampere but 'limited' on older GPUs; the matrix calls out where kernel optimizations are missing. For on-prem RTX class we sometimes need a different kernel selection which impacts latency 10-20%.
17:30 Tom (CTO): That's concerning—our on-prem fleet is mixed. How do you recommend we proceed?
17:42 Maya (SE): Two approaches: 1) Use hosted for initial bench and smoke tests to get quality baselines, then move to dedicated or private for production where we apply tuned kernels; 2) If you insist on on-prem from day one, we recommend a small compatibility sprint where we test a shortlist on your nodes and build kernels as needed. The sprint is usually 2-3 weeks.

20:05 Alex (AE): From a procurement perspective, what will trigger an enterprise engagement? Typical signals are >500k tokens/month, need for dedicated capacity, or on-prem deployment.
20:18 Tom (CTO): Likely we'll be in that band by Q3 if pilot metrics are good. Goal is GA in Q4.

21:00 Maya (SE): Security nit: for PHI we recommend private deployment with customer-managed keys; hosted can be used but requires strict contract terms and additional DPA clauses. We'll surface the options.
21:22 Sara (Security): We'll need to see the DPA and SOC2 scope. Also a network diagram for the private control plane.
21:35 Alex (AE): I'll share the DPA and network diagram links after the call.

23:05 Priya (ML): A practical question—how do you handle token counting and cost attribution when we use multiple models and reranking? We need per-route cost visibility.
23:20 Maya (SE): Console shows token-level breakdown by route and model; Optimize can generate suggestions like batching thresholds and cache TTLs to reduce token use. We'll include an example savings projection in the bench output.

25:40 Liam (Product): For product, we care about edge cases like hallucinations on older models; do you have safety/guardrails baked into the runtime or is that a prompt engineering responsibility?
25:55 Maya (SE): It's a shared responsibility. We offer moderation tooling, re-ranking flows, and safety policy hooks in the runtime. But prompt/eval work on your side is crucial. The bench will include safety tests and a precision/recall safety metric.

28:10 Alex (AE): Let's align on acceptance criteria for the pilot: 1) Quality threshold—achieve X on domain-specific ROUGE or a defined QA pass rate on 500 prompts; 2) Latency—p95 < 450ms for 512 tokens; 3) Cost—estimate under 25% above current baseline or justify tradeoffs. Are those reasonable?
28:35 Tom (CTO): Yes, those look reasonable. We'll quantify X (quality threshold) and share it by 03/08.

30:00 Maya (SE): Quick demo of Optimize: it suggests batch sizes and cache TTLs, flags models that are low token-efficiency. It also recommends quant profiles and shows simulated latency given your hardware profile. Note: simulator has +/- 10% variance compared to live runs.
30:32 Priya (ML): Do recommendations include kernel-level changes or just config?
30:38 Maya (SE): Mostly config and quant profiles; kernel builds are engineering tasks we handle as part of a compatibility sprint.

33:05 Tom (CTO): About the bench results format—we need raw metrics, per-prompt outputs, and a summary deck for stakeholders. Will you deliver all three?
33:16 Alex (AE): Yes, we deliver raw CSV/JSON outputs, a slide deck summarizing results, and a recommendation doc with cost modeling.

35:00 Priya (ML): For local bench runs, what's the memory footprint of the bench harness? We may need to spin up nodes.
35:10 Maya (SE): Bench runner is lightweight; model runtime is the heavy piece. We'll provide recommended instance types and GPU configs. For a 13B model with int8, plan for ~40-48GB GPU memory for comfortable runs depending on kernel and sequence length.

37:20 Sara (Security): One more on compliance: we need to ensure the private control plane can be deployed inside our VPC with no inbound from public internet. Is that supported?
37:33 Maya (SE): Yes, private control plane supports VPC-only deployment and can be air-gapped with an ops project. There are template playbooks for on-prem. We'll include the private deployment checklist and expected timeline (2-4 weeks for small pilots).

39:50 Alex (AE): Ok quick recap and owners. Alex will send pricing, DPA, and SOC2 docs. Maya will send bench harness and schedule deep-dive. Priya will send prompt set and SLOs. Tom will confirm timeline to procurement.

40:20 Tom (CTO): Sounds good. One ask: can you include a rough list of which open models you recommend starting with for clinical summarization?
40:32 Maya (SE): We'll recommend the 13B safety-tuned, the 6B med-tuned variant, and the 2.7B low-latency baseline. We'll add a note about specific tokenizers that handle medical abbreviations better.

42:10 Sara (Security): Please redact any customer-identifying info in the bench outputs for shared reports.
42:22 Alex (AE): Absolutely. We'll provide redaction steps and a sanitized example.

44:05 Priya (ML): Timeline check—if we get the bench artifacts and run the 500-prompt suite, how long till results?
44:16 Maya (SE): For hosted bench runs we can get preliminary within 3 business days; for private or on-prem runs it depends on your ops bandwidth, typically 1-2 weeks including kernel tweaks.

46:00 Alex (AE): Great, we'll aim for the follow-up deep dive week of 2027-03-15. Any final questions?
46:10 Liam (Product): None from me. Thanks all.
46:20 Tom (CTO): Thanks, talk soon.
46:30 End of transcript
